title: The yeast of the Pharisees (Matthew 16:1–12)
hookLine: one sour comment turns a whole group chat: how small things spread
tomorrow: who do people say you are, and who do you say you are?

cards: One sour comment lands in the group chat, and ten messages later the whole thread has turned. Nobody decided that. It spread.

Bakers know how: a pinch of starter worked into a new batch, and the whole dough rises. Jesus uses that picture in a boat. He's just crossed the lake with his friends, and partway over, someone realizes the problem.

teach.b: Into that worried boat, Jesus says: "Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees."
The disciples hear bread, only bread: "It is because we have taken no bread."

He reminds them of the loaves and the baskets, two crowds just fed, and then it clicks: "Then understood they how that he bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees."

A teaching, working its way through a person. And leaven itself isn't the villain: by the lake, he said the kingdom of heaven is like leaven too. Paul puts it in one line: "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump."
So the question is how small things spread in a heart, and the answer is: quietly, and all the way through.
A neighbor tradition knows this picture well. Before Passover, Jewish tradition clears the home of leaven, chametz, as the Torah commands.

And in the Talmud, a teacher named Rabbi Alexandri ends his prayer by asking what keeps us from doing God's will, and his answer includes the yeast in the dough. Shared ground: yeast as what quietly works its way through.

The honest difference: Matthew's leaven is a teaching to beware of; in the Talmud's prayer, the yeast is a pull inside a person. And in Jewish life, bread isn't bad the rest of the year. The clearing belongs to Passover.

how: Some Christians use unleavened bread at communion and some do not, and some churches read Paul's 'a little leaven' near Easter; some Jewish families search the house for leaven the night before Passover.

games.q: what does “the yeast of the pharisees” mean?
o: the bread the Pharisees baked for the temple
a teaching that spreads quietly through a person
a rule against eating bread on the sabbath

games.q: a little leaven — tap the pairs.

s: the disciples understood the leaven warning right away
they thought he meant bread: it is because we have taken no bread.
in Matthew, leaven is always a picture of something bad
by the lake, Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like leaven too.
Jewish tradition clears leaven from the home before Passover
the Torah commands it for the festival; the rest of the year, bread is ordinary food.

games.q: your team's group chat has turned cynical: one person's little digs about the boss, and now everyone does it. what's the leaven move?
o: call out the first one publicly, so everyone sees.
post one plain, fair word yourself, and skip the digs.
leave the chat for good; it's ruined now.
games.why: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump, and in Matthew 13 the kingdom works like leaven too. small things spread, sour or good.

practice: Catch one sour thought you've carried today, and name it once, plainly. Then count three small good things on your fingers, slowly, letting each one settle before the next. A little leaven works both ways.

wordCard.voice: The yeast of the Pharisees. Jesus' picture, in Matthew 16, for a teaching that works its way through a person the way leaven works through dough.

orig.note: Greek for leaven, in Matthew 16:6 and in the kingdom parable of 13:33.

carryVoice: Your line: a little leaven. Small things don't stay small, sour or good. Talk soon.
